content.question: Which articles deal with Fundamental Rights?
content.note:
Articles 12 to 35 in Part III of the Constitution deal with Fundamental Rights.
These rights are known as the Magna Carta of India.
Note: They are justiciable, meaning they can be enforced by courts if violated.

content.question: Who was the chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Indian Constitution?
content.note:
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee, which was the most important committee of the Constituent Assembly.
He is recognized as the 'Father of the Indian Constitution' for his role in framing the document.
Note: The committee had 7 members in total.

content.question: According to Dr. Ambedkar, which fundamental right is considered the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
content.note:
Dr. Ambedkar called the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.
He believed that a right without a remedy is a nullity; Article 32 makes fundamental rights real and effective. Other labels: It is also called the 'cornerstone' of the democratic system.

content.question: Who was the first Chairman of the Finance Commission of India?
content.note:
K.C. Neogy was the Chairman of the First Finance Commission (established in 1951).
The Finance Commission is a Constitutional Body under Article 280. Function: Its primary job is to recommend the distribution of tax revenues between the Union and the States.

content.question: Who is the ex-officio Chairperson of the NITI Aayog?
content.note:
The Prime Minister is the Ex-officio Chairperson of NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India).
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015.
Note: It acts as a policy 'Think Tank' for the Government of India, promoting Cooperative Federalism.

content.question: Which constitutional amendment act introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST)?
content.note:
The 101st Amendment Act, 2016 paved the way for the introduction of GST in India.
It replaced various indirect taxes with a single tax.
Note: GST came into effect on July 1, 2017. It required a special amendment because it involved the taxing powers of both Union and States.

content.question: Which Constitutional Amendment Act added Part IX (Panchayati Raj System) to the Constitution?
content.note:
The 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 (came into effect in 1993) added Part IX to the Constitution, titled 'The Panchayats'.
It gave Constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions. Related info: It also added the Eleventh Schedule, containing 29 functional items for Panchayats.

content.question: According to the Constitution, judges of the Supreme Court retire at what age?
content.note:
The retirement age for Supreme Court judges is 65 years.
This is mentioned in Article 124(2). Comparison: The retirement age for High Court judges is 62 years. There is no minimum age specified for appointment as a judge.

content.question: The Governor of an Indian state is appointed by whom?
content.note:
The President of India appoints the Governor of a state by warrant under his hand and seal.
The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President.
Note: Although the Governor is the head of the state executive, he/she is often described as an agent of the Central Government.

content.question: Which article provides the procedure for the impeachment of the President?
content.note:
Article 61 describes the procedure for the impeachment of the President for the 'violation of the Constitution'.
It is a quasi-judicial procedure in Parliament.
Note: To date, no President of India has ever been impeached.

content.question: Which constitutional amendment imposed a ban on political defections?
content.note:
The 52nd Amendment Act, 1985 introduced the Anti-Defection Law.
It added the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution to check the practice of legislators changing parties for power or office.
Note: The decision on disqualification is taken by the Presiding Officer of the House.

content.question: In every state, the Advocate General is appointed by whom?
content.note:
The Governor of the State appoints the Advocate General under Article 165.
The Advocate General is the highest law officer in the state (equivalent to the Attorney General at the Union level). Requirement: The person must be qualified to be appointed as a Judge of a High Court.

content.question: The Concurrent List in the Indian Constitution was adopted from which country?
content.note:
The Concurrent List (Seventh Schedule) was adopted from the Australian Constitution.
Both the Union and State governments can make laws on subjects in this list (e.g., Education, Forests).
Note: The Joint Sitting of Parliament and the Freedom of Trade/Commerce were also borrowed from Australia.

content.question: Under which article can a Money Bill not be introduced in the Legislative Council?
content.note:
A Money Bill cannot be introduced in the Legislative Council (Upper House of State) or the Rajya Sabha.
It can only be introduced in the Legislative Assembly (Lower House) on the recommendation of the Governor.
Note: The Legislative Council only has restricted powers to delay the bill for 14 days.

content.question: Which Act prevents disrespect to the national flag and national anthem?
content.answer: The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
content.note:
The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 prohibits the desecration of or insult to the country's national symbols.
This includes the National Flag, National Anthem, and the Constitution. Related info: This Act is an example of the legal enforcement of certain Fundamental Duties.

content.question: Which subject is included in the Eleventh Schedule?
content.note:
The Eleventh Schedule (73rd Amendment) includes subjects like Health and sanitation, agriculture, and rural housing.
These are the 29 matters over which Panchayats have jurisdiction.
Note: This was done to ensure basic services reach the grassroots level of rural India.

content.question: India adopted the concept of 'judicial review' from which country?
content.note:
The concept of Judicial Review was taken from the United States.
It allows the Judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders.
Note: Other features borrowed from the USA include the Preamble, Fundamental Rights, and Impeachment of the President.

content.question: What is the meaning of the Supreme Court's 'judicial review' function?
content.answer: To examine the constitutional validity of laws.
content.note:
The Judicial Review function allows the Judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders.
If a law is found to violate the Constitution, the Court can declare it null and void.
Note: This concept is primarily derived from the USA and ensures the supremacy of the Constitution.

content.question: How many times has the Preamble been amended?
content.note:
The Preamble has been amended only once since 1950.
This happened during the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976. Related info: That single amendment added the three words: Socialist, Secular, and Integrity.

content.question: Which Act stated that a member of the British Cabinet was appointed as Secretary of State for India?
content.note:
The Government of India Act, 1858 created the office of the Secretary of State for India.
This Act transferred the governance of India from the East India Company to the British Crown.
Note: The Secretary of State was a member of the British Cabinet and was responsible to the British Parliament.

content.question: When is the security deposit of a candidate forfeited?
content.answer: When the candidate fails to secure even one-sixth of the total valid votes cast.
content.note:
A candidate's security deposit is forfeited (lost) if they fail to secure at least one-sixth (1/6th) of the total valid votes polled in the constituency.
This rule is designed to discourage non-serious candidates from contesting elections.
Note: This applies to both Parliamentary and Assembly elections.

content.question: The world's longest written constitution belongs to which country?
content.note:
India possesses the world's longest written constitution.
Originally, it contained 395 Articles and 8 Schedules; currently, it has over 448 Articles. Factors: Its length is due to the geographical diversity of India, the historical influence of the 1935 Act, and the inclusion of both Administrative and Fundamental details.

content.question: When did the Constituent Assembly hold its first meeting?
content.note:
The Constituent Assembly held its first meeting on December 9, 1946, in the Constitution Hall (now Central Hall of Parliament).
Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, the oldest member, was elected as the temporary President.
Note: The Muslim League boycotted this first meeting.

content.question: Which Constitutional Amendment Act added Part IXA (Municipalities)?
content.note:
The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 (effective 1993) added Part IXA to the Constitution.
It gave constitutional status to Urban Local Bodies (Municipalities). Related info: It also added the Twelfth Schedule, which lists 18 functional items for municipalities.

content.question: Under which article can the President declare a Financial Emergency?
content.note:
Under Article 360, the President can declare a Financial Emergency if the financial stability or credit of India is threatened.
During such an emergency, the President can issue directions for the reduction of salaries of government officials.
Note: To date, a Financial Emergency has never been declared in India.

content.question: Which article relates to the definition of a Money Bill?
content.note:
Article 110 provides the definition of a Money Bill.
A bill is deemed a Money Bill if it contains provisions dealing with taxes, borrowing of money, or the Consolidated Fund of India.
Note: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha has the final authority to decide whether a bill is a Money Bill or not.

content.question: Which Article mentions 'equality of opportunity in matters relating to employment in the public sector'?
content.note:
Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State.
It prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or descent.
Note: This article also allows the State to provide reservations for backward classes.

content.question: The maximum possible interval between two sessions of Parliament is how many months?
content.note:
The maximum gap between two sessions of Parliament cannot exceed 6 months.
This means Parliament must meet at least twice a year. Related info: Usually, there are three sessions in a year: Budget, Monsoon, and Winter.

content.question: Which article defines the power of the President to grant pardons?
content.note:
Article 72 empowers the President to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment.
This power is independent of the Judiciary and is an executive power.
Note: The President can pardon a death sentence, whereas a Governor (under Article 161) cannot.

content.question: Who elects the Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
content.answer: All members of the Lok Sabha
content.note:
The Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha from amongst its own members.
The election date is fixed by the President.
Note: Usually, the Speaker remains in office during the life of the Lok Sabha, but they must resign if they cease to be a member of the House.

content.question: What is the purpose of the Fundamental Rights mentioned in the Indian Constitution?
content.note:
The Fundamental Rights (Part III) are intended to establish Political Democracy.
They protect the liberties and freedoms of citizens against the arbitrary invasion of the State. Comparison: While Fundamental Rights aim for political democracy, DPSPs aim for Social and Economic Democracy.

content.question: Under which article can President's Rule be declared in states?
content.note:
Article 356 allows for the imposition of President's Rule in a state if the constitutional machinery fails.
This is done on the recommendation of the Governor or if the President is satisfied otherwise.
Note: It is also known as a State Emergency or Constitutional Emergency.

content.question: The parliamentary form of government in India is borrowed from which country?
content.note:
The Parliamentary form of government was borrowed from the United Kingdom (England).
It is based on the Westminster model, where the executive is responsible to the legislature.
Note: Unlike Britain, where the Parliament is supreme, in India, the Constitution is supreme.

content.question: Which schedule contains provisions related to the Anti-Defection Law?
content.note:
The 10th Schedule contains provisions regarding disqualification on grounds of defection.
It was added by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985.
Note: It aims to provide stability to the government by preventing legislators from switching parties for personal gain.

content.question: Parliament can create or abolish a State Legislative Council on the recommendation of which body?
content.note:
Under Article 169, Parliament can create or abolish a Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) if the State Legislative Assembly passes a resolution to that effect by a special majority.
This gives the state the choice of having a unicameral or bicameral legislature.
Note: Currently, only a few states have a Legislative Council.

content.question: What does 'residuary powers' mean under the Indian Constitution?
content.answer: Powers which are not specifically enumerated in the Union List, State List, and Concurrent List.
content.note:
Residuary Powers refer to subjects that are not mentioned in any of the three lists (Union, State, or Concurrent).
In India, the power to make laws on these subjects rests with the Union Parliament. Related info: This feature is borrowed from the Canadian Constitution.
